content: The World Community Grid (WCG) is an initiative aimed at creating the largest public computing grid globally to address scientific research projects that benefit humanity. It was launched on November 16, 2004, and is funded and operated by IBM. The WCG client software is available for Windows, Linux, Mac OS X, and FreeBSD operating systems. By utilizing the idle processing power of computers worldwide, WCG has contributed to research on the human genome, HIV, dengue, muscular dystrophy, and cancer. To date, the organization has partnered with over 350 companies and organizations and has more than 345,000 registered user accounts. IBM and other research participants previously sponsored the United Devices Smallpox Research Grid Project, which used distributed computing to analyze the effectiveness of compounds against smallpox. This project screened 35 million potential drug molecules against smallpox proteins, identifying 44 strong treatment candidates. Based on the success of this project, IBM announced the creation of the World Community Grid on November 16, 2004, to support other humanitarian research projects. Linux support was added in November 2005 with the adoption of the open-source BOINC grid technology, which also powers projects like SETI@home and Climateprediction.net. Mac OS X and Linux are now officially supported platforms. As of January 6, 2008, WCG had 345,000 registered user accounts and over 864,000 registered computers, with over 134,000 years of computing time donated and more than 144 million work units completed. The WCG software operates by using the idle time of internet-connected computers to perform research calculations. Users install the WCG client software, which runs in the background, utilizing spare system resources to process work units. Once a work unit is completed, the results are sent back to WCG servers, and a new work unit is downloaded. To ensure accuracy, multiple copies of each work unit are distributed, and the results are validated against each other. Users can choose to display graphics from the current work unit as a screensaver or run the research software only in screensaver mode. Unlike other public computing grids that focus on a single project, WCG supports multiple humanitarian projects under one umbrella. Users are included in all projects by default but can opt out of specific ones. WCG also supports multiple grid infrastructures, with the open-source BOINC client available for all supported platforms. However, the scientific applications performing the calculations are closed-source to enhance security and prevent tampering with results. The WCG software increases CPU usage by utilizing unused processing time, which can sometimes lead to abnormal behavior on volunteered computers. Although the software is designed to be unobtrusive, it may still cause decreases in system performance or overheating. To mitigate these issues, the Grid MP software limits CPU usage to 60% by default, though this feature is not yet available for the BOINC client. If users experience persistent issues, they can pause or snooze the process temporarily, remove it from the startup list, or uninstall the WCG client software. User contributions to WCG are recorded, and statistics are publicly available. Contributions are measured in points, which are awarded based on the effort required to process each work unit. The BOINC client requests points based on software benchmarks, and WCG servers validate these claims by averaging the points from multiple computers processing the same work unit. Users can join teams to foster a sense of community and inspire competition, which ultimately increases the overall work done for the grid. WCG recognizes companies and organizations as partners if they promote the initiative within their networks. As of March 2, 2008, WCG had 376 partners. All computation results are released into the public domain and made available to the scientific community. IBM has also sponsored advertising campaigns to promote WCG. Active Projects: 1. FightAIDS@Home: This project focuses on testing potential drug molecules as protease inhibitors for HIV. The Scripps Research Institute published its first peer-reviewed paper on the results in April 2007. 2. Human Proteome Folding Phase 2 (HPF2): This project generates high-resolution protein models, focusing on human-secreted proteins, biomarkers, and proteins on cell surfaces, as well as the malaria-causing organism Plasmodium. 3. Discovering Dengue Drugs – Together: Sponsored by scientists at the University of Texas and the University of Chicago, this project tests potential antiviral drugs against flaviviruses in two phases. Phase 1 uses AutoDock software, while Phase 2 involves more computationally intensive screening. 4. AfricanClimate@Home: This project aims to refine climate models for Africa. 5. Help Conquer Cancer: Sponsored by the Ontario Cancer Institute, Princess Margaret Hospital, and University Health Network, this project uses X-ray crystallography to study cancer. Completed Projects: 1. Human Proteome Folding Phase 1 (HPF1): The first WCG project aimed to predict the structure of human proteins to better understand their functions and aid in disease research. Computing for this project was completed in July 2006. 2. Help Defeat Cancer: This project analyzed tissue microarrays to identify visual patterns correlated with treatment outcomes, potentially improving targeted cancer treatments. 3. Genome Comparison: Sponsored by the Brazilian research institution Fiocruz, this project compared gene sequences across organisms to identify functional similarities. 4. Help Cure Muscular Dystrophy Phase 1: Run by Décrypthon, this project investigated protein-protein interactions for 40,000 proteins, focusing on those involved in neuromuscular diseases. Upcoming Projects: 1. Help Cure Muscular Dystrophy Phase 2: Scheduled to start in early 2008, this phase will run on the BOINC platform, unlike Phase 1, which was limited to the Grid MP platform.
